# msvc_demangler - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/msvc-demangler/

## Expand description

msvc-demangler is a crate for Rust that can demangle C++ symbols which use the MSVC mangling scheme. These are emitted by the Microsoft C++ compiler for Windows as well as some others.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use msvc_demangler;
let flags = msvc_demangler::DemangleFlags::llvm();
let result = msvc_demangler::demangle("??_0klass@@QEAAHH@Z", flags).unwrap();
println!("{}", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#behavior)Behavior

It’s functionality is similar to `undname` on Windows and the underlying
`UnDecorateSymbolName` function.  Since Microsoft does not document the
mangling scheme this is likely not to be entirely accurate.  When unclear
the implementation tries to follow what LLVM does.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

This msvc-demangler is dual licensed under the MIT and the University of Illinois Open Source Licenses.

---

# msvc-demangler 0.11.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/msvc-demangler/latest

# msvc-demangler

msvc-demangler is a crate for Rust that can demangle C++ symbols which use the MSVC mangling scheme. These are emitted by the Microsoft C++ compiler for Windows as well as some others.

## Example

```
use msvc_demangler;
let flags = llvm;
let result = demangle.unwrap;
println!;
```
## Behavior

It's functionality is similar to `undname` on Windows and the underlying
`UnDecorateSymbolName` function.  Since Microsoft does not document the
mangling scheme this is likely not to be entirely accurate.  When unclear
the implementation tries to follow what LLVM does.

## License

This msvc-demangler is dual licensed under the MIT and the University of Illinois Open Source Licenses.

License: MIT/NCSA

# bitflags - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bitflags/^2/

## Expand description

Generate types for C-style flags with ergonomic APIs.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Add `bitflags` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.bitflags]
version = "2.13.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

The `bitflags` library defines a few Cargo features that you can opt-in to:

- `std`: Implement the- `Error`trait on error types used by- `bitflags`.
- `serde`: Support deriving- `serde`traits on generated flags types.
- `arbitrary`: Support deriving- `arbitrary`traits on generated flags types.
- `bytemuck`: Support deriving- `bytemuck`traits on generated flags types.

[§](https://docs.rs#generating-flags-types)Generating flags types

Use the [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro to generate flags types:

```
use bitflags::bitflags;
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
See the docs for the `bitflags` macro for the full syntax.

Also see the [ example_generated](https://docs.rs/example_generated/index.html) module for an example of what the

`bitflags` macro generates for a flags type.[§](https://docs.rs#externally-defined-flags)Externally defined flags

If you’re generating flags types for an external source, such as a C API, you can define
an extra unnamed flag as a mask of all bits the external source may ever set. Usually this would be all bits (`!0`):

```
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
        // The source may set any bits
        const _ = !0;
    }
}
```
Why should you do this? Generated methods like `all` and truncating operators like `!` only consider
bits in defined flags. Adding an unnamed flag makes those methods consider additional bits,
without generating additional constants for them. It helps compatibility when the external source
may start setting additional bits at any time. The [known and unknown bits](https://docs.rs#known-and-unknown-bits)
section has more details on this behavior.

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-derives)Custom derives

You can derive some traits on generated flags types if you enable Cargo features. The following libraries are currently supported:

- `serde`: Support- `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`, using text for human-readable formats, and a raw number for binary formats.
- `arbitrary`: Support- `#[derive(Arbitrary)]`, only generating flags values with known bits.
- `bytemuck`: Support- `#[derive(Pod, Zeroable)]`, for casting between flags values and their underlying bits values.

You can also define your own flags type outside of the [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro and then use it to generate methods.
This can be useful if you need a custom

`#[derive]` attribute for a library that `bitflags` doesn’t
natively support:```
#[derive(SomeTrait)]
pub struct Flags(u32);
bitflags! {
    impl Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#adding-custom-methods)Adding custom methods

The [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro supports attributes on generated flags types within the macro itself, while

`impl` blocks can be added outside of it:```
bitflags! {
    // Attributes can be applied to flags types
    #[repr(transparent)]
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
// Impl blocks can be added to flags types
impl Flags {
    pub fn as_u64(&self) -> u64 {
        self.bits() as u64
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-flags)Renaming flags

The [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro recognizes a special

`#[bitflags(flag_name = "<value>")]` attribute on flags values to rename them:```
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        // Add the attribute to a flag to change its name
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "a")]
        const A = 0b00000001;
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "b")]
        const B = 0b00000010;
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "c")]
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
When applied to a flag value, instead of using its identifier, like `A` as the name, it’ll use the given string. This
doesn’t affect the identifier of the constant itself, just the name recognized when parsing and formatting.

[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-flags-values)Working with flags values

Use generated constants and standard bitwise operators to interact with flags values:

```
// union
let ab = Flags::A | Flags::B;
// intersection
let a = ab & Flags::A;
// difference
let b = ab - Flags::A;
// complement
let c = !ab;
```
See the docs for the [ Flags](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html) trait for more details on operators and how they behave.

[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-and-parsing)Formatting and parsing

`bitflags` defines a text format that can be used to convert any flags value to and from strings.

See the [ parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html) module for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#specification)Specification

The terminology and behavior of generated flags types is
[specified in the source repository](https://github.com/bitflags/bitflags/blob/main/spec.md).
Details are repeated in these docs where appropriate, but is exhaustively listed in the spec. Some
things are worth calling out explicitly here.

[§](https://docs.rs#flags-types-flags-values-flags)Flags types, flags values, flags

The spec and these docs use consistent terminology to refer to things in the bitflags domain:

- **Bits type**: A type that defines a fixed number of bits at specific locations.
- **Flag**: A set of bits in a bits type that may have a unique name.
- **Flags type**: A set of defined flags over a specific bits type.
- **Flags value**: An instance of a flags type using its specific bits value for storage.

```
bitflags! {
    struct FlagsType: u8 {
//                    -- Bits type
//         --------- Flags type
        const A = 1;
//            ----- Flag
    }
}
let flag = FlagsType::A;
//  ---- Flags value
```
[§](https://docs.rs#known-and-unknown-bits)Known and unknown bits

Any bits in a flag you define are called *known bits*. Any other bits are *unknown bits*.
In the following flags type:

```
bitflags! {
    struct Flags: u8 {
        const A = 1;
        const B = 1 << 1;
        const C = 1 << 2;
    }
}
```
The known bits are `0b0000_0111` and the unknown bits are `0b1111_1000`.

`bitflags` doesn’t guarantee that a flags value will only ever have known bits set, but some operators
will unset any unknown bits they encounter. In a future version of `bitflags`, all operators will
unset unknown bits.

If you’re using `bitflags` for flags types defined externally, such as from C, you probably want all
bits to be considered known, in case that external source changes. You can do this using an unnamed
flag, as described in [externally defined flags](https://docs.rs#externally-defined-flags).

[§](https://docs.rs#zero-bit-flags)Zero-bit flags

Flags with no bits set should be avoided because they interact strangely with [ Flags::contains](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html#method.contains)
and

[. A zero-bit flag is always contained, but is never intersected. The names of zero-bit flags can be parsed, but are never formatted.](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html#method.intersects)

`Flags::intersects`[§](https://docs.rs#multi-bit-flags)Multi-bit flags

Flags that set multiple bits should be avoided unless each bit is also in a single-bit flag. Take the following flags type as an example:

```
bitflags! {
    struct Flags: u8 {
        const A = 1;
        const B = 1 | 1 << 1;
    }
}
```
The result of `Flags::A ^ Flags::B` is `0b0000_0010`, which doesn’t correspond to either
`Flags::A` or `Flags::B` even though it’s still a known bit.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [example_](https://docs.rs/example_generated/index.html)- generated
- This module shows an example of code generated by the macro. **IT MUST NOT BE USED OUTSIDE THIS CRATE**.
- [iter](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)
- Yield the bits of a source flags value in a set of contained flags values.
- [parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html)
- Parsing flags from text.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html)
- Generate a flags type.
- [bitflags_](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags_match.html)- match
- A macro that matches flags values, similar to Rust’s `match`statement.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Flag](https://docs.rs/struct.Flag.html)
- A defined flags value that may be named or unnamed.

# itoa - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/itoa/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides a fast conversion of integer primitives to decimal
strings. The implementation comes straight from [libcore](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1.92.0/library/core/src/fmt/num.rs#L190-L253) but avoids the
performance penalty of going through [ core::fmt::Formatter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/struct.Formatter.html).

See also [ zmij](https://github.com/dtolnay/zmij) for printing floating point primitives.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
fn main() {
    let mut buffer = itoa::Buffer::new();
    let printed = buffer.format(128u64);
    assert_eq!(printed, "128");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

The [itoa-benchmark](https://github.com/dtolnay/itoa-benchmark) compares this library and other Rust integer formatting
implementations across a range of integer sizes. The vertical axis in this
chart shows nanoseconds taken by a single execution of
`itoa::Buffer::new().format(value)` so a lower result indicates a faster
library.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)
- A correctly sized stack allocation for the formatted integer to be written into.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Integer](https://docs.rs/trait.Integer.html)
- An integer that can be written into an `itoa::Buffer`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |

# fakecloud_scheduler - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fakecloud-scheduler/0.31.0/fakecloud_scheduler/

## Expand description

AWS EventBridge Scheduler (`scheduler.amazonaws.com`).

Distinct from EventBridge Rules (`events.amazonaws.com`): Scheduler
is a standalone service with its own SDK, data model (Schedule,
ScheduleGroup, FlexibleTimeWindow, DeadLetterConfig,
ActionAfterCompletion), and REST-JSON protocol.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [delivery](https://docs.rs/delivery/index.html)
- Target delivery + DLQ routing for fired schedules.
- [expr](https://docs.rs/expr/index.html)
- Schedule expression parsing and matching.
- [persistence](https://docs.rs/persistence/index.html)
- Snapshot load helper for the scheduler state.
- [simulation](https://docs.rs/simulation/index.html)
- Test-only helpers that drive the Scheduler firing pipeline from introspection endpoints. Lets integration tests bypass the wall clock by poking a specific schedule and observing delivery.
- [ticker](https://docs.rs/ticker/index.html)
- Background firing loop for EventBridge Scheduler.

# polkadot_node_core_chain_api - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-core-chain-api/32.0.0/polkadot_node_core_chain_api/

## Expand description

Implements the Chain API Subsystem

Provides access to the chain data. Every request may return an error.
At the moment, the implementation requires `Client` to implement `HeaderBackend`,
we may add more bounds in the future if we will need e.g. block bodies.

Supported requests:

- Block hash to number
- Block hash to header
- Block weight (cumulative)
- Finalized block number to hash
- Last finalized block number
- Ancestors

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainApiSubsystem.html)- ApiSubsystem
- The Chain API Subsystem implementation.

# pivx_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pivx-rpc/0.3.0/pivx_rpc/

## Expand description

PIVX SDK: typed JSON-RPC client for pivxd with first-class support for shielded (SHIELD/Sapling) balances and transactions.

```
use pivx_rpc::{Auth, PivxClient, ShieldRecipient, ShieldWatcher, WatchOptions};
let client = PivxClient::new(
    "http://127.0.0.1:51473",
    Auth::UserPass { user: "rpcuser".into(), pass: "rpcpass".into() },
)?;
// Watch a shielded address via its viewing key (no spend key needed).
let imported = client.import_sapling_viewing_key("p-view-key...", None, None).await?;
let mut watcher = ShieldWatcher::new(&client, WatchOptions {
    addresses: vec![imported.address],
    ..Default::default()
});
let events = watcher.poll().await?; // first poll primes silently
// Send shielded funds (node wallet holds the keys and builds the proof).
let txid = client
    .shield_send_many(
        pivx_rpc::FromAddress::AnyShield,
        &[ShieldRecipient::new("ps1...", 1.5).with_memo("hello")],
    )
    .await?;
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockHeader.html)- Header
- Verbose block header (`getblockheader`, verbose=true). For the raw serialized header use`get_block`with verbosity 0.
- [Blockchain](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockchainInfo.html)- Info
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainTip.html)- Tip
- One entry of `getchaintips`.
- [Decoded](https://docs.rs/struct.DecodedTransaction.html)- Transaction
- Decoded transaction (`decoderawtransaction`, verbose`getrawtransaction`).
- [Imported](https://docs.rs/struct.ImportedSaplingKey.html)- Sapling - Key
- Result of `importsaplingkey`/`importsaplingviewingkey`.
- [List](https://docs.rs/struct.ListSinceBlock.html)- Since - Block
- Result of `list_since_block`. PIVX omits the`removed`array.
- [List](https://docs.rs/struct.ListTransaction.html)- Transaction
- Element of `list_transactions`/`list_since_block`(long form: the listtransactions fields plus the embedded wallet-tx fields).
- [Pivx](https://docs.rs/struct.PivxClient.html)- Client
- Async JSON-RPC client for a pivxd node.
- [PrevTx](https://docs.rs/struct.PrevTx.html)
- Previous-output spec for `sign_raw_transaction`.
- [Received](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceivedShieldNote.html)- Shield - Note
- Received note, as returned by `listreceivedbyshieldaddress`.
- [Script](https://docs.rs/struct.ScriptPubKey.html)- PubKey
- Script of a transaction output (`gettxout`, decoded-tx vout).
- [Script](https://docs.rs/struct.ScriptSig.html)- Sig
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldNote.html)- Note
- Unspent shielded note, as returned by `listshieldunspent`.

- Recipient entry for `shieldsendmany`/`rawshieldsendmany`.
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldTxOutput.html)- TxOutput

- Decrypted view of a shielded transaction (`viewshieldtransaction`).
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldWatcher.html)- Watcher
- Polls the node and reports `ShieldEvent`
- [Sign](https://docs.rs/struct.SignError.html)- Error
- [Sign](https://docs.rs/struct.SignRawTransactionResult.html)- RawTransaction - Result
- Result of `sign_raw_transaction`.
- [Transaction](https://docs.rs/struct.Transaction.html)
- Wallet’s record of a transaction (`gettransaction`).
- [Transaction](https://docs.rs/struct.TransactionDetail.html)- Detail
- Short detail element embedded in `gettransaction`.
- [TxInput](https://docs.rs/struct.TxInput.html)
- Input spec for `create_raw_transaction`.

- Unspent output details (`gettxout`); the call returns`None`when spent or not found.
- [Unspent](https://docs.rs/struct.Unspent.html)
- [Validate](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidateAddress.html)- Address
- Result of `validate_address`. Only`isvalid`is guaranteed; the rest depend on validity and address type (transparent vs shield).
- [Vin](https://docs.rs/struct.Vin.html)
- Input of a decoded transaction. Coinbase inputs carry `coinbase`; every other input carries`txid`/`vout`/`script_sig`.
- [Vout](https://docs.rs/struct.Vout.html)
- Output of a decoded transaction.
- [Wallet](https://docs.rs/struct.WalletInfo.html)- Info
- [Watch](https://docs.rs/struct.WatchOptions.html)- Options
- Options for `ShieldWatcher`

# odcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/odcs/0.9.1/odcs/

## Expand description

Reference implementation of the Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS).

This is a **reference implementation** — not the normative ODCS specification.
The upstream standard is maintained at
[bitol-io/open-data-contract-standard](https://github.com/bitol-io/open-data-contract-standard).

[§](https://docs.rs#user-documentation)User documentation

[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline)Pipeline

`ODCS Document → Parser → Canonical Object Model → Validator → Diagnostics`[§](https://docs.rs#stable-api)Stable API

Use root re-exports only (`parse`, `validate`, `parse_and_validate`, `DataContract`,
`ContractSet`, `Registry`, `diff`, …). Internal modules (`parser`, `validation`, `model`, …)
are `#[doc(hidden)]` and not semver-stable. See the
[public API guide](https://odcs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/implementation/public-api.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling)Error handling

- `parse`- `parse_and_validate`- `DiagnosticReport`- `ParseResult`
- `parse_file`- `DataContract::from_file`- `miette::Result`for I/O errors
- `ParseResult::into_contract`- `parse_strict`- `Result<DataContract, DiagnosticReport>`after parse and validation

Match on diagnostic [ codes](https://docs.rs/codes/index.html) and

`object_ref`, not message text.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use odcs::{parse, validate, DocumentFormat};
let yaml = br#"
version: "1.0.0"
apiVersion: "v3.1.0"
kind: "DataContract"
id: "example"
status: "draft"
"#;
let result = parse(yaml, DocumentFormat::Yaml);
let contract = result.contract.expect("parse succeeded");
let report = validate(&contract);
assert!(report.is_valid());
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use compatibility::`- [diff](https://docs.rs/compatibility/fn.diff.html);
- `pub use compatibility::`- [ChangeKind](https://docs.rs/compatibility/enum.ChangeKind.html);
- `pub use compatibility::`- [CompatibilityChange](https://docs.rs/compatibility/struct.CompatibilityChange.html);
- `pub use compatibility::`- [CompatibilityReport](https://docs.rs/compatibility/struct.CompatibilityReport.html);
- `pub use contract_set::`- [load_set](https://docs.rs/contract_set/fn.load_set.html);
- `pub use contract_set::`- [load_set_with_registry](https://docs.rs/contract_set/fn.load_set_with_registry.html);
- `pub use contract_set::`- [parse_and_validate_set](https://docs.rs/contract_set/fn.parse_and_validate_set.html);
- `pub use contract_set::`- [parse_and_validate_set_with_registry](https://docs.rs/contract_set/fn.parse_and_validate_set_with_registry.html);
- `pub use contract_set::`- [validate_set](https://docs.rs/contract_set/fn.validate_set.html);
- `pub use contract_set::`- [ContractSet](https://docs.rs/contract_set/struct.ContractSet.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [cli](https://docs.rs/cli/index.html)
- Command-line interface.
- [codes](https://docs.rs/codes/index.html)
- Standardized `odcs:`diagnostic identifiers.
- [compatibility](https://docs.rs/compatibility/index.html)

# fakecloud_resource_groups - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fakecloud-resource-groups/0.31.0/fakecloud_resource_groups/

## Expand description

AWS Resource Groups (`resource-groups`) restJson1 service for fakecloud.

Batch 1: the full 23-operation control plane from the AWS Smithy model –
group lifecycle (Create/Get/Update/Delete/ListGroups), resource queries
(GetGroupQuery/UpdateGroupQuery), explicit membership
(GroupResources/UngroupResources/ListGroupResources), search
(SearchResources), group configuration (Get/PutGroupConfiguration), tagging
(Tag/Untag/GetTags), account settings (Get/UpdateAccountSettings), grouping
statuses (ListGroupingStatuses), and tag-sync tasks
(Start/Get/List/CancelTagSyncTask). Every operation is backed by real,
account-partitioned, persisted state with AWS-shaped
`arn:aws:resource-groups:...:group/<name>/<id>` ARNs.

Query-based membership resolution (evaluating a `TAG_FILTERS_1_0` /
`CLOUDFORMATION_STACK_1_0` query against live resources) depends on the
cross-service tag index that ships with the Resource Groups Tagging API
batch; until then a query-based group resolves to its explicitly associated
members. Explicit `GroupResources` membership is fully real now.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use service::`- [ResourceGroupsService](https://docs.rs/service/struct.ResourceGroupsService.html);
- `pub use state::`- [ResourceGroupsState](https://docs.rs/state/struct.ResourceGroupsState.html);
- `pub use state::`- [RESOURCE_GROUPS_SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA_VERSION](https://docs.rs/state/constant.RESOURCE_GROUPS_SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA_VERSION.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [persistence](https://docs.rs/persistence/index.html)
- Snapshot save/load for Resource Groups state.
- [service](https://docs.rs/service/index.html)
- Resource Groups restJson1 dispatch + operation handlers.
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- Account-partitioned, serializable state for AWS Resource Groups.

# sim_lib_logic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-logic/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_logic/

## Expand description

Logic behavior for the SIM runtime: clauses, unification, and queries.

The kernel defines the `Shape`, eval-policy, and codec contracts; this crate
supplies the concrete logic organ (a clause database, unifier, constraint
solving, and a query/stream surface).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use policy::`- [LogicPolicy](https://docs.rs/policy/struct.LogicPolicy.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [builtins](https://docs.rs/builtins/index.html)
- Browseable logic builtin bindings.
- [policy](https://docs.rs/policy/index.html)
- Eval-policy adapter for running logic queries through a `sim_kernel::Cx`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Clause](https://docs.rs/struct.Clause.html)
- A parsed logic clause: a head goal plus an optional list of body goals.
- [Clause](https://docs.rs/struct.ClauseId.html)- Id
- Stable identifier assigned to a clause when it is added to a database.
- [Logic](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicConfig.html)- Config
- Aggregate tuning for the logic organ, threaded through every query.
- [LogicDb](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicDb.html)
- An indexed store of logic `Clause`
- [Logic](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicEnv.html)- Env
- A unification substitution: bindings from logic variables to terms.
- [Logic](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicLib.html)- Lib
- The loadable logic organ: shapes, functions, and database/config state.
- [Logic](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicLimits.html)- Limits
- Resource ceilings that bound a single logic query.
- [Logic](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicQuery.html)- Query
- A goal paired with the `LogicConfig`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- Whether the unifier runs the occurs check when binding a variable.
- [Search](https://docs.rs/enum.SearchStrategy.html)- Strategy
- Order in which the resolver explores pending goal states.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_logic_lib.html)- logic_ - lib
- Installs the `LogicLib``cx`, idempotently.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_clause_expr.html)- clause_ - expr
- Parses a `(fact head)`or`(rule head body)`expression into a`Clause`
- [query](https://docs.rs/fn.query.html)
- Resolves `goal`against`db`and returns the answers as a logic stream.
- [query_](https://docs.rs/fn.query_all.html)- all
- Resolves `goal`against`db`and returns all answers up to`limit`.
- [query_](https://docs.rs/fn.query_all_with_builtins.html)- all_ - with_ - builtins
- Resolves `goal`with an explicit builtin table.
- [realize_](https://docs.rs/fn.realize_logic.html)- logic
- Resolves `goal`against the installed logic database and returns the result.
- [unify_](https://docs.rs/fn.unify_exprs.html)- exprs
- Unifies two expressions and reports the result as a kernel `ShapeMatch`.

# yatrosci_sparse - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-sparse/0.1.0/yatrosci_sparse/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scirs-sparse-matrices)SciRS Sparse Matrices

Sparse matrix data structures and algorithms for scientific computing,
providing functionality equivalent to `scipy.sparse`.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

This crate provides:

- Sparse matrix formats: CSR, CSC, COO, DOK, LIL, DIA, BSR
- Sparse matrix construction utilities
- Sparse linear algebra operations
- Format conversion between sparse representations
- Sparse-dense and sparse-sparse operations

[§](https://docs.rs#sparse-formats)Sparse Formats

| Format | Description | Best For |
|---|---|---|
| CSR | Compressed Sparse Row | Row slicing, matrix-vector products |
| CSC | Compressed Sparse Column | Column slicing, arithmetic operations |
| COO | Coordinate Format | Incremental construction |
| DOK | Dictionary of Keys | Random access insertion |
| LIL | List of Lists | Row-wise construction |
| DIA | Diagonal Format | Diagonal/banded matrices |
| BSR | Block Sparse Row | Block-structured matrices |

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use yatrosci_sparse::{CsrMatrix, CooMatrix};
use ndarray::array;
// Create COO matrix and convert to CSR
let mut coo = CooMatrix::<f64>::new(3, 3);
coo.push(0, 0, 1.0);
coo.push(1, 1, 2.0);
coo.push(2, 2, 3.0);
let csr = coo.to_csr();
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use construct::`- [block_diag](https://docs.rs/construct/fn.block_diag.html);
- `pub use construct::`- [diags](https://docs.rs/construct/fn.diags.html);

- `pub use construct::`- [hstack](https://docs.rs/construct/fn.hstack.html);

# msvc-demangler 0.11.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/msvc-demangler/0.11.0

# msvc-demangler

msvc-demangler is a crate for Rust that can demangle C++ symbols which use the MSVC mangling scheme. These are emitted by the Microsoft C++ compiler for Windows as well as some others.

## Example

```
use msvc_demangler;
let flags = llvm;
let result = demangle.unwrap;
println!;
```
## Behavior

It's functionality is similar to `undname` on Windows and the underlying
`UnDecorateSymbolName` function.  Since Microsoft does not document the
mangling scheme this is likely not to be entirely accurate.  When unclear
the implementation tries to follow what LLVM does.

## License

This msvc-demangler is dual licensed under the MIT and the University of Illinois Open Source Licenses.

License: MIT/NCSA

---

# msvc_demangler - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/msvc-demangler/0.11.0/target-redirect/msvc_demangler/

## Expand description

msvc-demangler is a crate for Rust that can demangle C++ symbols which use the MSVC mangling scheme. These are emitted by the Microsoft C++ compiler for Windows as well as some others.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use msvc_demangler;
let flags = msvc_demangler::DemangleFlags::llvm();
let result = msvc_demangler::demangle("??_0klass@@QEAAHH@Z", flags).unwrap();
println!("{}", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#behavior)Behavior

It’s functionality is similar to `undname` on Windows and the underlying
`UnDecorateSymbolName` function.  Since Microsoft does not document the
mangling scheme this is likely not to be entirely accurate.  When unclear
the implementation tries to follow what LLVM does.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

This msvc-demangler is dual licensed under the MIT and the University of Illinois Open Source Licenses.

# msvc_demangler - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/msvc-demangler/0.11.0/msvc_demangler/index.html

## Expand description

msvc-demangler is a crate for Rust that can demangle C++ symbols which use the MSVC mangling scheme. These are emitted by the Microsoft C++ compiler for Windows as well as some others.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use msvc_demangler;
let flags = msvc_demangler::DemangleFlags::llvm();
let result = msvc_demangler::demangle("??_0klass@@QEAAHH@Z", flags).unwrap();
println!("{}", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#behavior)Behavior

It’s functionality is similar to `undname` on Windows and the underlying
`UnDecorateSymbolName` function.  Since Microsoft does not document the
mangling scheme this is likely not to be entirely accurate.  When unclear
the implementation tries to follow what LLVM does.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

This msvc-demangler is dual licensed under the MIT and the University of Illinois Open Source Licenses.

The intersection of a source flags value with the complement of a target flags value (`&!`).

This method is not equivalent to `self & !other` when `other` has unknown bits set.
`difference` won’t truncate `other`, but the `!` operator will.

#### fn [sub_assign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.SubAssign.html#tymethod.sub_assign)(&mut self, other: Self)

The intersection of a source flags value with the complement of a target flags value (`&!`).

This method is not equivalent to `self & !other` when `other` has unknown bits set.
`difference` won’t truncate `other`, but the `!` operator will.

# demangle in msvc_demangler - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/msvc-demangler/0.11.0/msvc_demangler/fn.demangle.html

`pub fn demangle(input: &`[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.str.html), flags: [DemangleFlags](https://docs.rs/struct.DemangleFlags.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)>```
4fn main() {
5    let args: Vec<String> = env::args().collect();
6    if args.len() != 2 {
7        println!("{} <symbol>", args[0]);
8        std::process::exit(1);
9    }
10
11    match demangle(&args[1], DemangleFlags::COMPLETE) {
12        Ok(s) => {
13            println!("{}", s);
14        }
15        Err(err) => {
16            eprintln!("error: {:?}", err);
17            std::process::exit(1);
18        }
19    }
20}
```

# msvc_demangler - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/msvc-demangler/latest/msvc_demangler/

## Expand description

msvc-demangler is a crate for Rust that can demangle C++ symbols which use the MSVC mangling scheme. These are emitted by the Microsoft C++ compiler for Windows as well as some others.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use msvc_demangler;
let flags = msvc_demangler::DemangleFlags::llvm();
let result = msvc_demangler::demangle("??_0klass@@QEAAHH@Z", flags).unwrap();
println!("{}", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#behavior)Behavior

It’s functionality is similar to `undname` on Windows and the underlying
`UnDecorateSymbolName` function.  Since Microsoft does not document the
mangling scheme this is likely not to be entirely accurate.  When unclear
the implementation tries to follow what LLVM does.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

This msvc-demangler is dual licensed under the MIT and the University of Illinois Open Source Licenses.

---

# bitflags 2.13.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bitflags/^2

# bitflags

`bitflags` generates flags enums with well-defined semantics and ergonomic end-user APIs.

You can use `bitflags` to:

- provide more user-friendly bindings to C APIs where flags may or may not be fully known in advance.
- generate efficient options types with string parsing and formatting support.

You can't use `bitflags` to:

-
guarantee only bits corresponding to defined flags will ever be set. `bitflags`allows access to the underlying bits type so arbitrary bits may be set.
-
define bitfields. `bitflags`only generates types where set bits denote the presence of some combination of flags.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.13.0"
```
and this to your source code:

```
use bitflags;
```
## Example

Generate a flags structure:

```
use bitflags;
// The `bitflags!` macro generates `struct`s that manage a set of flags.
bitflags!
```
## Cargo features

The `bitflags` library defines a few Cargo features that you can opt-in to:

- `std`: Implement the- `Error`trait on error types used by- `bitflags`.
- `serde`: Support deriving- `serde`traits on generated flags types.
- `arbitrary`: Support deriving- `arbitrary`traits on generated flags types.
- `bytemuck`: Support deriving- `bytemuck`traits on generated flags types.

Also see [ bitflags_derive](https://github.com/bitflags/bitflags-derive) for other flags-aware traits.

## Rust Version Support

The minimum supported Rust version is documented in the `Cargo.toml` file.
This may be bumped in minor releases as necessary.

---

# itoa 1.0.18 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/itoa/^1.0

# itoa

This crate provides a fast conversion of integer primitives to decimal strings.
The implementation comes straight from [libcore](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1.92.0/library/core/src/fmt/num.rs#L190-L253) but avoids the performance
penalty of going through [ core::fmt::Formatter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/struct.Formatter.html).

See also [ zmij](https://github.com/dtolnay/zmij) for printing floating point primitives.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Example

```
```
## Performance

The [itoa-benchmark](https://github.com/dtolnay/itoa-benchmark) compares this library and other Rust integer formatting
implementations across a range of integer sizes. The vertical axis in this chart
shows nanoseconds taken by a single execution of
`itoa::Buffer::new().format(value)` so a lower result indicates a faster
library.

# msvc-demangler 0.10.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/msvc-demangler/0.10.1

# msvc-demangler

msvc-demangler is a crate for Rust that can demangle C++ symbols which use the MSVC mangling scheme. These are emitted by the Microsoft C++ compiler for Windows as well as some others.

## Example

```
use msvc_demangler;
let flags = llvm;
let result = demangle.unwrap;
println!;
```
## Behavior

It's functionality is similar to `undname` on Windows and the underlying
`UnDecorateSymbolName` function.  Since Microsoft does not document the
mangling scheme this is likely not to be entirely accurate.  When unclear
the implementation tries to follow what LLVM does.

## License

This msvc-demangler is dual licensed under the MIT and the University of Illinois Open Source Licenses.

License: MIT/NCSA

---

# bitflags 2.13.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bitflags/2.13.0

# bitflags

`bitflags` generates flags enums with well-defined semantics and ergonomic end-user APIs.

You can use `bitflags` to:

- provide more user-friendly bindings to C APIs where flags may or may not be fully known in advance.
- generate efficient options types with string parsing and formatting support.

You can't use `bitflags` to:

-
guarantee only bits corresponding to defined flags will ever be set. `bitflags`allows access to the underlying bits type so arbitrary bits may be set.
-
define bitfields. `bitflags`only generates types where set bits denote the presence of some combination of flags.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.13.0"
```
and this to your source code:

```
use bitflags;
```
## Example

Generate a flags structure:

```
use bitflags;
// The `bitflags!` macro generates `struct`s that manage a set of flags.
bitflags!
```
## Cargo features

The `bitflags` library defines a few Cargo features that you can opt-in to:

- `std`: Implement the- `Error`trait on error types used by- `bitflags`.
- `serde`: Support deriving- `serde`traits on generated flags types.
- `arbitrary`: Support deriving- `arbitrary`traits on generated flags types.
- `bytemuck`: Support deriving- `bytemuck`traits on generated flags types.

Also see [ bitflags_derive](https://github.com/bitflags/bitflags-derive) for other flags-aware traits.

## Rust Version Support

The minimum supported Rust version is documented in the `Cargo.toml` file.
This may be bumped in minor releases as necessary.

# arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arbitrary/^1.0/

## Expand description

The `Arbitrary` trait crate.

This trait provides an [ Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html) trait to
produce well-typed, structured values, from raw, byte buffers. It is
generally intended to be used with fuzzers like AFL or libFuzzer. See the

[trait’s documentation for details on automatically deriving, implementing, and/or using the trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`Arbitrary`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [size_](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html)- hint
- Utilities for working with and combining the results of
`Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [unstructured](https://docs.rs/unstructured/index.html)
- Wrappers around raw, unstructured bytes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [MaxRecursion](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)- Reached
- Error indicating that the maximum recursion depth has been reached while calculating `Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)
- A source of unstructured data.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An enumeration of buffer creation errors

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A `Result`with the error type fixed as`arbitrary::Error`.

---

# bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.12/

## Expand description

This crate gives small utilities for casting between plain data types.

[§](https://docs.rs#basics)Basics

Data comes in five basic forms in Rust, so we have five basic casting functions:

- `T`uses- `cast`
- `&T`uses- `cast_ref`
- `&mut T`uses- `cast_mut`
- `&[T]`uses- `cast_slice`
- `&mut [T]`uses- `cast_slice_mut`

Depending on the function, the [ NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) and/or

[traits are used to maintain memory safety.](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`**Historical Note:** When the crate first started the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait was used
instead, and so you may hear people refer to that, but it has the strongest
requirements and people eventually wanted the more fine-grained system, so
here we are. All types that impl

`Pod` have a blanket impl to also support
`NoUninit` and `AnyBitPattern`. The traits unfortunately do not have a
perfectly clean hierarchy for semver reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

Some casts will never fail, and other casts might fail.

- `cast::<u32, f32>`always works (and- `f32::from_bits`
- `cast_ref::<[u8; 4], u32>`might fail if the specific array reference given at runtime doesn’t have alignment 4.

In addition to the “normal” forms of each function, which will panic on
invalid input, there’s also `try_` versions which will return a `Result`.

If you would like to statically ensure that a cast will work at runtime you
can use the `must_cast` crate feature and the `must_` casting functions. A
“must cast” that can’t be statically known to be valid will cause a
compilation error (and sometimes a very hard to read compilation error).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-your-own-types)Using Your Own Types

All the functions listed above are guarded by the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait, which is a
sub-trait of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`If you enable the crate’s `derive` feature then these traits can be derived
on your own types. The derive macros will perform the necessary checks on
your type declaration, and trigger an error if your type does not qualify.

The derive macros might not cover all edge cases, and sometimes they will
error when actually everything is fine. As a last resort you can impl these
traits manually. However, these traits are `unsafe`, and you should
carefully read the requirements before using a manual implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The crate supports Rust 1.34 when no features are enabled, and so there’s cargo features for thing that you might consider “obvious”.

The cargo features **do not** promise any particular MSRV, and they may
increase their MSRV in new versions.

- `derive`: Provide derive macros for the various traits.
- `extern_crate_alloc`: Provide utilities for- `alloc`related types such as Box and Vec.
- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`and- `zeroable_atomics`: Provide more- `Zeroable`
- `pod_saturating`: Provide more- `Pod`- `Zeroable`
- `wasm_simd`and- `aarch64_simd`: Support more SIMD types.
- `min_const_generics`: Provides appropriate impls for arrays of all lengths instead of just for a select list of array lengths.
- `must_cast`: Provides the- `must_`functions, which will compile error if the requested cast can’t be statically verified.
- `const_zeroed`: Provides a const version of the- `zeroed`function.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

- `pack1`- `bytemuck`-compatible packed little-endian, big-endian and native-endian integer and floating point number types.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use checked::`- [CheckedBitPattern](https://docs.rs/checked/trait.CheckedBitPattern.html);
- `pub use`- [allocation](https://docs.rs/allocation/index.html)::*;- `extern_crate_alloc`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [allocation](https://docs.rs/allocation/index.html)- `extern_crate_alloc`
- Stuff to boost things in the `alloc`crate.
- [checked](https://docs.rs/checked/index.html)
- Checked versions of the casting functions exposed in crate root
that support `CheckedBitPattern`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [offset_](https://docs.rs/macro.offset_of.html)- of
- Find the offset in bytes of the given `$field`of`$Type`. Requires an already initialized`$instance`value to work with.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [PodCast](https://docs.rs/enum.PodCastError.html)- Error
- The things that can go wrong when casting between `Pod`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AnyBit](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)- Pattern
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types that are valid for any bit pattern.
- [Contiguous](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html)
- A trait indicating that:
- [NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types with no uninit (or padding) bytes.
- [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data”.
- [PodIn](https://docs.rs/trait.PodInOption.html)- Option
- Trait for types which are [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).
- [Transparent](https://docs.rs/trait.TransparentWrapper.html)- Wrapper
- A trait which indicates that a type is a `#[repr(transparent)]`wrapper around the`Inner`value.
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)
- Trait for types that can be safely created with
`zeroed`
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroableInOption.html)- InOption
- Trait for types which are [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_of.html)- of
- Re-interprets `&T`as`&[u8]`.
- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_of_mut.html)- of_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut T`as`&mut [u8]`.
- [cast](https://docs.rs/fn.cast.html)
- Cast `A`into`B`
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_mut.html)- mut
- Cast `&mut A`into`&mut B`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_ref.html)- ref
- Cast `&A`into`&B`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_slice.html)- slice
- Cast `&[A]`into`&[B]`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_slice_mut.html)- slice_ - mut
- Cast `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`.
- [fill_](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_zeroes.html)- zeroes
- Fill all bytes of `slice`with zeroes (see`Zeroable`
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes.html)- bytes
- Re-interprets `&[u8]`as`&T`.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes_mut.html)- bytes_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut [u8]`as`&mut T`.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast.html)- cast - `must_cast`
- Cast `A`into`B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_mut.html)- cast_ - mut - `must_cast`
- Convert a `&mut A`into`&mut B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_ref.html)- cast_ - ref - `must_cast`
- Convert `&A`into`&B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_slice.html)- cast_ - slice - `must_cast`
- Convert `&[A]`into`&[B]`(possibly with a change in length) if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_slice_mut.html)- cast_ - slice_ - mut - `must_cast`
- Convert `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`(possibly with a change in length) if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_align_to.html)- align_ - to
- As `align_to``Pod`
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_align_to_mut.html)- align_ - to_ - mut
- As `align_to_mut``Pod`
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_read_unaligned.html)- read_ - unaligned
- Reads the slice into a `T`value.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast.html)- cast
- Try to cast `A`into`B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_mut.html)- cast_ - mut
- Try to convert a `&mut A`into`&mut B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_ref.html)- cast_ - ref
- Try to convert a `&A`into`&B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_slice.html)- cast_ - slice
- Try to convert `&[A]`into`&[B]`(possibly with a change in length).
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_slice_mut.html)- cast_ - slice_ - mut
- Try to convert `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`(possibly with a change in length).
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_from_bytes.html)- from_ - bytes
- Re-interprets `&[u8]`as`&T`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_from_bytes_mut.html)- from_ - bytes_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut [u8]`as`&mut T`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_pod_read_unaligned.html)- pod_ - read_ - unaligned
- Reads from the bytes as if they were a `T`.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_zeroes.html)- zeroes
- Fill all bytes of `target`with zeroes (see`Zeroable`
- [zeroed](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroed.html)- `const_zeroed`
- Same as `Zeroable::zeroed``const fn`const.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [AnyBit](https://docs.rs/derive.AnyBitPattern.html)- Pattern - `derive`
- Derive the `AnyBitPattern`trait for a struct

- Derive the `Contiguous`trait for an enum

- Derive the `NoUninit`trait for a struct or enum
- [Pod](https://docs.rs/derive.Pod.html)- `derive`
- Derive the `Pod`trait for a struct
- [Transparent](https://docs.rs/derive.TransparentWrapper.html)- Wrapper - `derive`
- Derive the `TransparentWrapper`trait for a struct
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/derive.Zeroable.html)- `derive`
- Derive the `Zeroable`trait for a type.

# serde_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/^1.0.228/

## Expand description

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The `serde_core` crate contains Serde’s trait definitions with **no support
for #[derive()]**.

In crates that derive an implementation of `Serialize` or `Deserialize`, you
must depend on the [ serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) crate, not

`serde_core`.In crates that handwrite implementations of Serde traits, or only use them
as trait bounds, depending on `serde_core` is permitted. But `serde`
re-exports all of these traits and can be used for this use case too. If in
doubt, disregard `serde_core` and always use `serde`.

Crates that depend on `serde_core` instead of `serde` are able to compile in
parallel with `serde_derive` even when `serde`’s “derive” feature is turned on,
as shown in the following build timings.

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde` |

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde_core` |

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

---

# bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.12.2/

## Expand description

instead, and so you may hear people refer to that, but it has the strongest
requirements and people eventually wanted the more fine-grained system, so
here we are. All types that impl

`Pod` have a blanket impl to also support
`NoUninit` and `AnyBitPattern`. The traits unfortunately do not have a
perfectly clean hierarchy for semver reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

Some casts will never fail, and other casts might fail.

- `cast::<u32, f32>`always works (and- `f32::from_bits`
- `cast_ref::<[u8; 4], u32>`might fail if the specific array reference given at runtime doesn’t have alignment 4.

In addition to the “normal” forms of each function, which will panic on
invalid input, there’s also `try_` versions which will return a `Result`.

If you would like to statically ensure that a cast will work at runtime you
can use the `must_cast` crate feature and the `must_` casting functions. A
“must cast” that can’t be statically known to be valid will cause a
compilation error (and sometimes a very hard to read compilation error).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-your-own-types)Using Your Own Types

All the functions listed above are guarded by the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait, which is a
sub-trait of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`If you enable the crate’s `derive` feature then these traits can be derived
on your own types. The derive macros will perform the necessary checks on
your type declaration, and trigger an error if your type does not qualify.

The derive macros might not cover all edge cases, and sometimes they will
error when actually everything is fine. As a last resort you can impl these
traits manually. However, these traits are `unsafe`, and you should
carefully read the requirements before using a manual implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The crate supports Rust 1.34 when no features are enabled, and so there’s cargo features for thing that you might consider “obvious”.

The cargo features **do not** promise any particular MSRV, and they may
increase their MSRV in new versions.

- `derive`: Provide derive macros for the various traits.
- `extern_crate_alloc`: Provide utilities for- `alloc`related types such as Box and Vec.
- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`and- `zeroable_atomics`: Provide more- `Zeroable`
- `pod_saturating`: Provide more- `Pod`- `Zeroable`
- `wasm_simd`and- `aarch64_simd`: Support more SIMD types.
- `min_const_generics`: Provides appropriate impls for arrays of all lengths instead of just for a select list of array lengths.
- `must_cast`: Provides the- `must_`functions, which will compile error if the requested cast can’t be statically verified.
- `const_zeroed`: Provides a const version of the- `zeroed`function.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

- `pack1`- `bytemuck`-compatible packed little-endian, big-endian and native-endian integer and floating point number types.

# rustversion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustversion/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides macros for conditional compilation according to rustc
compiler version, analogous to [ #[cfg(...)]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg-attribute) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute)

`#[cfg_attr(...)]`[§](https://docs.rs#selectors)Selectors

- `#[rustversion::stable]`
 True on any stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::stable(1.34)]`
 True on exactly the specified stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::beta]`
 True on any beta compiler.
- `#[rustversion::nightly]`
 True on any nightly compiler or dev build.
- `#[rustversion::nightly(2025-01-01)]`
 True on exactly one nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(1.34)]`
 True on that stable release and any later compiler, including beta and nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(2025-01-01)]`
 True on that nightly and all newer ones.
- `#[rustversion::before(`- *version or date*- `)]`
 Negative of- *#[rustversion::since(...)]*.
- `#[rustversion::not(`- *selector*- `)]`
 Negative of any selector; for example- *#[rustversion::not(nightly)]*.
- `#[rustversion::any(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if any of the comma-separated selectors is true; for example- *#[rustversion::any(stable, beta)]*.
- `#[rustversion::all(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if all of the comma-separated selectors are true; for example- *#[rustversion::all(since(1.31), before(1.34))]*.
- `#[rustversion::attr(`- *selector*- `,`- *attribute*- `)]`
 For conditional inclusion of attributes; analogous to- `cfg_attr`.
- `rustversion::cfg!(`- *selector*- `)`
 An expression form of any of the above attributes; for example- *if rustversion::cfg!(any(stable, beta)) { ... }*.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-cases)Use cases

Providing additional trait impls as types are stabilized in the standard library
without breaking compatibility with older compilers; in this case Pin<P>
stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2019/02/28/Rust-1.33.0.html#pinning):

```
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
use std::pin::Pin;
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
impl<P: MyTrait> MyTrait for Pin<P> {
    /* ... */
}
```
Similar but for language features; the ability to control alignment greater than
1 of packed structs was stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md#version-1330-2019-02-28).

```
#[rustversion::attr(before(1.33), repr(packed))]
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.33), repr(packed(2)))]
struct Six(i16, i32);
fn main() {
    println!("{}", std::mem::align_of::<Six>());
}
```
Augmenting code with `const` as const impls are stabilized in the standard
library. This use of `const` as an attribute is recognized as a special case
by the rustversion::attr macro.

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.32), const)]
fn duration_as_days(dur: Duration) -> u64 {
    dur.as_secs() / 60 / 60 / 24
}
```
Emitting Cargo cfg directives from a build script. Note that this requires
listing `rustversion` under `[build-dependencies]` in Cargo.toml, not
`[dependencies]`.

```
// build.rs
fn main() {
    if rustversion::cfg!(since(1.36)) {
        println!("cargo:rustc-cfg=no_std");
    }
}
```
```
// src/lib.rs
#![cfg_attr(no_std, no_std)]
#[cfg(no_std)]
extern crate alloc;
```

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)- reader - `std`
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from an I/O stream of JSON.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)- slice
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from bytes of JSON text.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html)- str
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from a string of JSON text.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_value.html)- value

- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html)- string - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a String of JSON.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string_pretty.html)- string_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a pretty-printed String of JSON.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_value.html)- value
- Convert a `T`into`serde_json::Value`which is an enum that can represent any valid JSON data.
- [to_vec](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)- `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a JSON byte vector.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec_pretty.html)- vec_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a pretty-printed JSON byte vector.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)- writer - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as JSON into the I/O stream.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer_pretty.html)- writer_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as pretty-printed JSON into the I/O stream.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Alias for a `Result`with the error type`serde_json::Error`.
